claim: A subset of glioblastoma harbors a bias towards hypomethylation at defined differentially methylated regions.
source: We describe a subset of glioblastoma, the most prevalent malignant adult brain tumour, harbouring a bias towards hypomethylation at defined differentially methylated regions.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding based on the study's analysis of DNA methylation data.

claim: The epigenetic signature of hypomethylation correlates with an enrichment for an astrocytic gene signature.
source: This epigenetic signature correlates with an enrichment for an astrocytic gene signature, which together with the identification of enriched predicted binding sites of transcription factors known to cause demethylation and to be involved in astrocytic/glial lineage specification, point to a shared ontogeny between these glioblastomas and astroglial progenitors.
evidence: The abstract states this correlation based on the study's analysis of methylation and transcriptional data.

claim: Enriched predicted binding sites of transcription factors known to cause demethylation and to be involved in astrocytic/glial lineage specification are identified in hypomethylated glioblastomas.
source: This epigenetic signature correlates with an enrichment for an astrocytic gene signature, which together with the identification of enriched predicted binding sites of transcription factors known to cause demethylation and to be involved in astrocytic/glial lineage specification, point to a shared ontogeny between these glioblastomas and astroglial progenitors.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on motif enrichment analysis performed in the study.

claim: The hypomethylation bias and astrocytic signature enrichment point to a shared ontogeny between these glioblastomas and astroglial progenitors.
source: This epigenetic signature correlates with an enrichment for an astrocytic gene signature, which together with the identification of enriched predicted binding sites of transcription factors known to cause demethylation and to be involved in astrocytic/glial lineage specification, point to a shared ontogeny between these glioblastomas and astroglial progenitors.
evidence: The abstract presents this as an interpretation of the combined findings from methylation, transcriptional, and motif analyses.

claim: Increased invasiveness characterizes the subset of glioblastoma with hypomethylation bias and astrocytic signature enrichment.
source: At functional level, increased invasiveness, at least in part mediated by SRPX2, and macrophage infiltration characterise this subset of glioblastoma.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on xenograft experiments and invasion assays described in the study.

claim: SRPX2 at least in part mediates the increased invasiveness in the subset of glioblastoma with hypomethylation bias.
source: At functional level, increased invasiveness, at least in part mediated by SRPX2, and macrophage infiltration characterise this subset of glioblastoma.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on SRPX2 knockdown experiments showing reduced invasion.

claim: Macrophage infiltration characterizes the subset of glioblastoma with hypomethylation bias and astrocytic signature enrichment.
source: At functional level, increased invasiveness, at least in part mediated by SRPX2, and macrophage infiltration characterise this subset of glioblastoma.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data and immunohistochemistry.

claim: Glioblastoma is a highly aggressive brain tumour.
source: Glioblastoma IDH-wildtype (now renamed glioblastoma) is a highly aggressive brain tumour (Wen and Kesari, 2008), with an extremely poor prognosis of 15 months' median survival from diagnosis (Alcantara Llaguno and Parada, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Glioblastoma has an extremely poor prognosis of 15 months' median survival from diagnosis.
source: Glioblastoma IDH-wildtype (now renamed glioblastoma) is a highly aggressive brain tumour (Wen and Kesari, 2008), with an extremely poor prognosis of 15 months' median survival from diagnosis (Alcantara Llaguno and Parada, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Glioblastoma is the most prevalent primary adult brain tumour with an annual occurrence of approximately five cases per 100,000 people.
source: Glioblastoma is also the most prevalent primary adult brain tumour with an annual occurrence of approximately five cases per 100,000 people (Wen and Kesari, 2008; Omuro and DeAngelis, 2013) and a mean diagnosis age of 64 (Bush et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The mean diagnosis age for glioblastoma is 64.
source: Glioblastoma is also the most prevalent primary adult brain tumour with an annual occurrence of approximately five cases per 100,000 people (Wen and Kesari, 2008; Omuro and DeAngelis, 2013) and a mean diagnosis age of 64 (Bush et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: GICs 19, 30, 31, and 17 had over 60% hypo-methylated DMRs.
source: GICs 19, 30, 31, and 17 stood out as they had over 60% hypo-methylated DMRs, and together had a statistically significant larger proportion of hypo-methylated probes and DMRs as compared to the other six GICs in the cohort.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the DNA methylation analysis of the cohort.

claim: GICs 19, 30, 31, and 17 had a statistically significant larger proportion of hypo-methylated probes and DMRs compared to the other six GICs in the cohort.
source: GICs 19, 30, 31, and 17 stood out as they had over 60% hypo-methylated DMRs, and together had a statistically significant larger proportion of hypo-methylated probes and DMRs as compared to the other six GICs in the cohort.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from statistical analysis of the DNA methylation data.

claim: Three of the four B-GICs belonged to the RTKI (Proneural) subgroup and one to the RTKII (Classical) subgroup.
source: This subgrouping did not reflect the known DNA methylation-based classification of Sturm, 2012; three of the four B-GICs belonged to the RTKI (Proneural) subgroup and one to the RTKII (Classical) subgroup.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the classification analysis of the GICs.

claim: The proportion of hypo-methylated and hyper-methylated DMRs was exaggerated when patient-specific probes and DMRs were considered.
source: Noticeably, the proportion of hypo-methylated and hyper-methylated DMRs was exaggerated, when patient-specific probes and DMRs were considered (Figure 1A, right panel).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Principal component 1 largely separated GICs by hypo-methylation bias, with three out of four B-GICs (19, 30, and 31) clustering together.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the 5000 most variable DNA methylation probes across all GICs in our cohort showed that principal component 1 (PC1) largely separated GICs by hypo-methylation bias, with three out of four B-GICs (19, 30, and 31, highlighted) clustering together on the left of the plot and all remaining GICs to the right (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from PCA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The top 100 probes driving PC1 had much lower beta values in B-GICs 19, 30, and 31 relative to all other GICs.
source: A heatmap dendrogram of the beta values of the top 100 probes driving PC1 showed that these probes had much lower beta values in B-GICs 19, 30, and 31 relative to all other GICs, reflecting the separate cluster observed in the PCA (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the heatmap analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The hypo-methylation bias was GIC-driven, and not caused by the iNSC comparator.
source: This observation suggested that the hypo-methylation bias was GIC-driven, and not caused by the iNSC comparator, a conclusion which was confirmed when we performed non-syngeneic comparisons between each GIC and each of the iNSCs in our cohort (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from non-syngeneic comparison analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 46.5% of HGCC GICs were found to have a hypo-methylation bias.
source: Using this threshold, 46.5% of HGCC GICs were found to have a hypo-methylation bias.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis of the HGCC cohort.

claim: The proportion of B-GICs in the HGCC cohort (46.5%) was comparable with the proportion in the study's smaller cohort (45.5% had greater than 50% DMRs and 36.4% had 60% DMRs).
source: This was comparable with the proportion in our smaller cohort where we found 5/11 (45.5%) had greater than <50% DMRs and 4/11 (36.4%) had <60% DMRs.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between the two cohorts.

claim: PC1 separated HGCC GICs on the extent of their hypo-methylation bias with very high B-GICs clustering to the right, and those with no bias clustering to the left.
source: PCA of the 5000 most variable methylation probes across the HGCC GICs showed that PC1 separated patients on the extent of their hypo-methylation bias with very high B-GICs clustering to the right, and those with no bias clustering to the left (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from PCA analysis of the HGCC cohort shown in Figure 1F.

claim: TCGA subgroup classification confirmed no enrichment for a specific subgroup in B-GICs.
source: TCGA subgroup classification confirmed no enrichment for a specific subgroup (of the 33 GICs deemed to have a hypo-methylation bias, 15 were Mesenchymal, 4 Proneural, 6 Classical, and 8 Neural), in keeping with the interpretation that the hypo-methylation bias observed is spread across the known glioblastoma subgroups.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from TCGA subgroup classification analysis.

claim: Tumours 19, 30, 31, and 17 showed a greater proportion of hypo-methylated DMRs than the remaining six comparisons when FFPE tumour tissue was used as the neoplastic comparator.
source: Once again, tumours 19, 30, 31, and 17 showed a greater proportion of hypo-methylated DMRs than the remaining six comparisons (Figure 1H, left panel), and the proportion of hypo-methylated DMRs increased when only considering patient-specific DMRs (Figure 1H, right panel).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of FFPE tissue shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The hypo-methylation bias is not induced in GIC by in vitro culture as it was confirmed in the respective tumour tissue.
source: Importantly, we have shown that the hypo-methylation bias is not induced in GIC by in vitro culture as it was confirmed in the respective tumour tissue.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the FFPE tissue analysis.

claim: PCA based on the top 20% most variably expressed genes recapitulated the grouping of GICs observed at DNA methylome level.
source: PCA based on the top 20% most variably expressed genes recapitulated the grouping of GICs observed at DNA methylome level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) with PC1 largely distinguishing the B-GIC and nB-GIC groups.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from PCA analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Patient-matched pairs of GICs and iNSCs did not reveal a bias in the directionality of differentially expressed genes.
source: Despite these differences at transcriptome level, patient-matched pairs of GICs and iNSCs did not reveal a bias in the directionality of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the hypo-methylation bias does not translate to a bias in gene up- or down-regulation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The hypo-methylation bias does not translate to a bias in gene up- or down-regulation.
source: Despite these differences at transcriptome level, patient-matched pairs of GICs and iNSCs did not reveal a bias in the directionality of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), indicating that the hypo-methylation bias does not translate to a bias in gene up- or down-regulation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the differential expression analysis.

claim: Known genes associated with epigenetic remodelling or DNA methylation such as DNMTs or TETs were not identified within the DEGs.
source: Known genes associated with epigenetic remodelling or DNA methylation such as DNMTs or TETs were not identified within the DEGs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Clustering of the 500 most variably expressed miRNAs did not recapitulate the grouping of samples into B-GICs and nB-GICs.
source: Clustering of the 500 most variably expressed miRNAs did not recapitulate the grouping of samples into B-GICs and nB-GICs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from miRNA expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Comparisons between GICs and iNSCs did not reveal a bias in directionality of expression of differentially expressed miRNAs.
source: Similarly, comparisons between GICs and iNSCs did not reveal a bias in directionality of expression of differentially expressed miRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from miRNA differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Five miRNAs (miR-1275, miR-4443, miR-196, miR-5100, and miR-1268) were differentially expressed in the same direction in all B-GICs.
source: Interestingly though, we identified five miRNAs differentially expressed in the same direction in all B-GICs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from miRNA differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Silencing of miR-1275 induces GFAP expression in glioblastoma cells.
source: Silencing of miR-1275 induces GFAP (an astrocyte marker) expression in glioblastoma cells (Mai et al., 2019), and its down-regulation was associated with oligodendroglia differentiation of tumour cells (Katsushima et al., 2012) – similarly in our dataset this miRNA is down-regulated.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Down-regulation of miR-1275 was associated with oligodendroglia differentiation of tumour cells.
source: Silencing of miR-1275 induces GFAP (an astrocyte marker) expression in glioblastoma cells (Mai et al., 2019), and its down-regulation was associated with oligodendroglia differentiation of tumour cells (Katsushima et al., 2012) – similarly in our dataset this miRNA is down-regulated.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: miR-1275 is down-regulated in B-GICs.
source: Silencing of miR-1275 induces GFAP (an astrocyte marker) expression in glioblastoma cells (Mai et al., 2019), and its down-regulation was associated with oligodendroglia differentiation of tumour cells (Katsushima et al., 2012) – similarly in our dataset this miRNA is down-regulated.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the miRNA expression analysis.

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway is a key regulator of astrocyte differentiation and activation.
source: The JAK/STAT pathway, which is known to be a key regulator of astrocyte differentiation and activation (Xiao et al., 2010; He et al., 2005; Bonni et al., 1997; Ceyzériat et al., 2016), is thought to be up-regulated by miR-4443, which is down-regulated in our GICs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: miR-4443 is thought to up-regulate the JAK/STAT pathway.
source: The JAK/STAT pathway, which is known to be a key regulator of astrocyte differentiation and activation (Xiao et al., 2010; He et al., 2005; Bonni et al., 1997; Ceyzériat et al., 2016), is thought to be up-regulated by miR-4443, which is down-regulated in our GICs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative connection based on literature.

claim: miR-4443 is down-regulated in B-GICs.
source: The JAK/STAT pathway, which is known to be a key regulator of astrocyte differentiation and activation (Xiao et al., 2010; He et al., 2005; Bonni et al., 1997; Ceyzériat et al., 2016), is thought to be up-regulated by miR-4443, which is down-regulated in our GICs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the miRNA expression analysis.

claim: miR-196 plays an essential role in neural development as it helps regulate Homeobox (HOX) genes.
source: Finally, miR-196, which is up-regulated in B-GICs, plays an essential role in neural development as it helps regulate Homeobox (HOX) genes (Sehm et al., 2009), some of which have been shown to play a role in astrocyte biology (Vivinetto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Some HOX genes have been shown to play a role in astrocyte biology.
source: Finally, miR-196, which is up-regulated in B-GICs, plays an essential role in neural development as it helps regulate Homeobox (HOX) genes (Sehm et al., 2009), some of which have been shown to play a role in astrocyte biology (Vivinetto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: miR-196 is up-regulated in B-GICs.
source: Finally, miR-196, which is up-regulated in B-GICs, plays an essential role in neural development as it helps regulate Homeobox (HOX) genes (Sehm et al., 2009), some of which have been shown to play a role in astrocyte biology (Vivinetto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the miRNA expression analysis.

claim: Hypo-methylated DMRs from B-GICs compared against DMRs from all GIC-iNSC comparisons showed enrichment for binding motifs of zinc-finger proteins, HOX genes, HNF4, KLF, NFI, and DLX.
source: Firstly, the hypo-methylated DMRs from the B-GICs-iNSC comparison were compared against DMRs from all GIC-iNSC comparisons. The top five enriched motifs were matches for an array of zinc-finger proteins, HOX genes, and families of factors such as hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 (HNF4), Kruppel-like factors (KLF), nuclear factor I (NFI), and distal-less homeobox (DLX) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NFI, ETV4, DLX, and KLF have been previously linked to astrocyte/glial differentiation.
source: We noticed that some of these TFs, namely NFI, ETV4, DLX, and KLF have been previously linked to astrocyte/glial differentiation (Sanosaka et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2015; Marshall and Goldman, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Hypo-methylated DMRs from B-GICs compared to hypo-methylated DMRs from nB-GICs showed enrichment for binding motifs of PLAGL1, NFI family members, ETV4, and SOX family members.
source: The top five enriched motifs were found to be matches for some of the same TFs identified in the first analysis such as PLAGL1, NFI family members, and ETS variant transcription factor 4 (ETV4) (Figure 2B). Interestingly, the fifth ranked enriched motif from this analysis was a strong match for members of the SOX family, known to be involved in cellular differentiation and neural development (Kamachi and Kondoh, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SOX family members are known to be involved in cellular differentiation and neural development.
source: Interestingly, the fifth ranked enriched motif from this analysis was a strong match for members of the SOX family, known to be involved in cellular differentiation and neural development (Kamachi and Kondoh, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: PLAGL1, NFI, or ETV4 were not identified in the motif enrichment analysis of hyper-methylated DMRs from B-GICs.
source: Importantly, PLAGL1, NFI, or ETV4 were not identified in this analysis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: iAPCs co-expressed the astrocytic lineage marker CD44 and the neural progenitor marker NESTIN.
source: DNA methylome and transcriptome were analysed in five different progenitor lines at a differentiation stage, where cells co-expressed the astrocytic lineage marker CD44 (Liu et al., 2004) and the neural progenitor marker NESTIN (Bernal and Arranz, 2018), in keeping with a astrocytic progenitor state (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: iAPCs acquired a pro-inflammatory response upon IL6 treatment, not observed in iNSC.
source: Acquisition of a pro-inflammatory response upon IL6 treatment (Tcw et al., 2017), not observed in iNSC, and brisk proliferative activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D), confirmed the astrocytic commitment of the cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from IL6 treatment experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: iAPCs showed brisk proliferative activity.
source: Acquisition of a pro-inflammatory response upon IL6 treatment (Tcw et al., 2017), not observed in iNSC, and brisk proliferative activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D), confirmed the astrocytic commitment of the cells.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from proliferation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: iAPCs and iOPCs were epigenetically and transcriptionally distinct from one another and from the cells from which they were derived.
source: Inspection of the DNA methylation and RNAseq datasets obtained from these cells confirmed that iAPCs and iOPCs were epigenetically and transcriptionally distinct from one another and from the cells from which they were derived (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from DNA methylation and RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: iAPCs were enriched for an astrocytic signature.
source: Furthermore, both cell types were found to be enriched for an astrocytic and oligodendrocyte signature, respectively (Figure 2F, G, H).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ssGSEA analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: iOPCs were enriched for an oligodendrocyte signature.
source: Furthermore, both cell types were found to be enriched for an astrocytic and oligodendrocyte signature, respectively (Figure 2F, G, H).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ssGSEA analysis shown in Figure 2G, H.

claim: The top enriched motif in hypo-methylated DMRs from iAPCs was a strong match for ETV4.
source: The top five 'de novo' enriched motifs were matches for binding sites previously found to be enriched in the comparison of hypo-methylated DMRs from B-GICs (Figure 2A, B). In particular, the top enriched motif was a strong match for ETV4 confirming the link between this factor and hypo-methylated astrocyte associated loci (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The NFI binding motif was the fifth-ranked enriched motif among the 'known matches' in hypo-methylated DMRs from iAPCs.
source: The NFI binding motif was the fifth-ranked enriched motif among the 'known matches' from Homer (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: ETV4 and NFI binding sites were not identified as enriched in hypo-methylated DMRs from iOPCs-iNSC comparison.
source: ETV4 and NFI binding sites were not identified as enriched in either the 'de novo' or 'known matches' when motif enrichment analysis was performed on hypo-methylated DMRs from iOPCs-iNSC comparison against all other DMRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Hypo-methylated DMRs in iOPCs as compared to iNSCs were enriched for the binding sites of ZIC genes, HOX genes, SOX genes, and an array of zinc-finger proteins.
source: Instead, hypo-methylated DMRs in iOPCs as compared to iNSCs were enriched for the binding sites of ZIC genes, HOX genes, SOX genes, and an array of zinc-finger proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: All GICs scored highly for the early-RG signature with little variability between lines.
source: All GICs scored highly for the early-RG signature with little variability between lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), likely reflecting the high degree of transcriptional similarity between GICs and NSCs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ssGSEA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Four out of four B-GICs (17, 19, 30, and 31) had significantly higher enrichment scores for the ACS than the two OPC signatures.
source: Four out of four B-GICs (17, 19, 30, and 31) had significantly higher enrichment scores for the ACS than the two OPC signatures (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ssGSEA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The pattern of ACS and OPC signature enrichment was not retained in the bulk tumours.
source: We further scored matching bulk FFPE tumour tissues for the ACS and two OPC signatures and found that the pattern of enrichment was not retained in the bulk tumours with very few tumours scoring highly for the ACS and the majority of tumour scoring highly for the OPC signatures (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ssGSEA analysis of FFPE tissue shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 55% of the samples were found to be enriched for the ACS in the HGCC dataset.
source: Given these criteria, 55% of the samples were found to be enriched for the ACS in the HGCC dataset, compared to approximately 64% in our cohort, hence confirming an ACS enrichment in an independent GIC cohort.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ssGSEA analysis of the HGCC cohort.

claim: Approximately 64% of samples in the study's cohort were enriched for the ACS.
source: Given these criteria, 55% of the samples were found to be enriched for the ACS in the HGCC dataset, compared to approximately 64% in our cohort, hence confirming an ACS enrichment in an independent GIC cohort.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from ssGSEA analysis of the study's cohort.

claim: A subset of tumours (MGH105, MGH114, MGH143, ND2, and ND4) scored higher for the ACS than the two OPC signatures based on pseudo-bulk analysis of scRNAseq data.
source: Firstly, by treating all the single cancer cells' expression as pseudo-bulk tumour tissue, we were able to identify a subset of tumours, which scored higher for the ACS than the two OPC signatures (MGH105, MGH114, MGH143, ND2, and ND4) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from pseudo-bulk ssGSEA analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The same tumours found to have a higher ACS enrichment score based on pseudo-bulk analysis had increased proportion of ACS cells: 75.07% ± 19.40% compared to 26.26% ± 11.69% in the remaining tumours.
source: Encouragingly the same tumours found to have a higher ACS enrichment score based on the pseudo-bulk analysis, had increased proportion of ACS cells: 75.07% ± 19.40% compared to 26.26% ± 11.69% in the remaining tumours (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from single-cell analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A significant positive correlation was found between GIC ACS signature enrichment scores and the percentage of hypo-methylated DMRs in the study's cohort.
source: A significant positive correlation was found between GIC ACS signature enrichment scores and the percentage of hypo-methylated DMRs in both our (Figure 3D, L) and in the HGCC cohorts (Figure 3E, M), raising the possibility that the two findings could be causally related.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claim: A significant positive correlation was found between GIC ACS signature enrichment scores and the percentage of hypo-methylated DMRs in the HGCC cohort.
source: A significant positive correlation was found between GIC ACS signature enrichment scores and the percentage of hypo-methylated DMRs in both our (Figure 3D, L) and in the HGCC cohorts (Figure 3E, M), raising the possibility that the two findings could be causally related.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1M.

claim: Of the 465 DEGs identified in the comparison of BE-GICs versus nBE-GICs in the study's cohort, 47 were part of the ACS.
source: Of the 465 DEGs (Figure 3F), 47 were part of the ACS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I) (Fisher's exact test, p-value < 0.00001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Of the 902 DEGs identified in the comparison of BE-GICs versus nBE-GICs in the HGCC cohort, 52 were present in the ACS.
source: The same differential expression comparison in the HGCC cohort identified a total of 902 DEGs (Figure 3G), of which a significant number (52) were also present in the ACS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J) (Fisher's exact test, p-value < 0.00001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: RUNX2 was up-regulated in BE-GICs as compared to the nBE-GICs in the HGCC cohort.
source: When considering the top DEGs between the two groups in the HGCC cohort, RUNX2 was up-regulated whilst OLIG2 was down-regulated in BE-GICs as compared to the nBE-GICs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from differential expression analysis of the HGCC cohort.

claim: OLIG2 was down-regulated in BE-GICs as compared to the nBE-GICs in the HGCC cohort.
source: When considering the top DEGs between the two groups in the HGCC cohort, RUNX2 was up-regulated whilst OLIG2 was down-regulated in BE-GICs as compared to the nBE-GICs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from differential expression analysis of the HGCC cohort.

claim: RUNX2 has been shown to drive astrocytic differentiation.
source: This is an interesting finding, as RUNX2 has been shown to drive astrocytic differentiation, and OLIG2 is a well-known master regulator of oligodendroglia differentiation (Tiwari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: OLIG2 is a well-known master regulator of oligodendroglia differentiation.
source: This is an interesting finding, as RUNX2 has been shown to drive astrocytic differentiation, and OLIG2 is a well-known master regulator of oligodendroglia differentiation (Tiwari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: An overlap of 105 genes from the 465 DEGs identified in the study's cohort and the 902 DEGs identified in the HGCC cohort was found.
source: An overlap of 105 genes from the 465 DEGs identified in our cohort and the 902 DEGs identified in the HGCC cohort was found (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K) (Fisher's exact test, p-value < 0.00001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparison of DEG lists shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Pathway analysis on the two lists of DEGs revealed a shared enrichment for pathways associated with the extracellular matrix, morphogenesis, cell adhesion, angiogenesis, locomotion, wound healing, and cytokine signalling.
source: Finally, pathway analysis on the two lists of DEGs revealed a shared enrichment for pathways associated with the extracellular matrix, morphogenesis, cell adhesion, angiogenesis, locomotion, wound healing, and cytokine signalling (Figure 3H), suggesting a deregulation of these pathways in BE-GICs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from pathway analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Xenografts derived from BE-GICs showed increased invasiveness.
source: Xenografts derived from BE-GICs showed increased invasiveness (Figure 4A, B, C), despite having a smaller tumour core (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C, D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from xenograft analysis shown in Figure 4A, B, C.

claim: Xenografts derived from BE-GICs had a smaller tumour core.
source: Xenografts derived from BE-GICs showed increased invasiveness (Figure 4A, B, C), despite having a smaller tumour core (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C, D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from xenograft analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C, D.

claim: GLIPR1, SRPX2, and LIF were identified as genes present in the ACS and differentially expressed in both GIC versus iNSC and iAPC versus iNSC comparisons.
source: GLI pathogenesis related 1 (GLIPR1), sushi repeat containing protein X-linked 2 (SRPX2), and leukaemia inhibitory factor (LIF) were identified (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the differential expression analysis strategy shown in Figure 4D.

claim: GLIPR1 has been found to regulate migration and invasion of glioma cells.

claim: LIF has been shown to contribute to the maintenance of glioma-initiating cell self-renewal.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: LIF has been shown to help mediate astrocyte differentiation.
source: Moreover, LIF has been shown to help mediate astrocyte differentiation (Nakashima et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: SRPX2 was up-regulated in the comparisons between iNSC and iAPC across all patients.
source: Analysis of the pattern of expression of SRPX2 in our dataset found that it was up-regulated in the comparisons between iNSC and iAPC across all patients, and its expression was specifically higher in the GICs of patients 19 and 31 (Figure 4E), as expected.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from expression analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SRPX2 expression was specifically higher in the GICs of patients 19 and 31.
source: Analysis of the pattern of expression of SRPX2 in our dataset found that it was up-regulated in the comparisons between iNSC and iAPC across all patients, and its expression was specifically higher in the GICs of patients 19 and 31 (Figure 4E), as expected.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from expression analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SRPX2 was more highly expressed in glioblastoma tumour tissue as compared to non-tumour brain tissue according to TCGA data.
source: Given our limited cohort size, the deregulation of SRPX2 was further validated in other datasets and found that it was more highly expressed in glioblastoma tumour tissue as compared to non-tumour brain tissue according to TCGA data (Figure 4F) and in BE-GICs from the HGCC cohort (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SRPX2 was more highly expressed in BE-GICs from the HGCC cohort.
source: Given our limited cohort size, the deregulation of SRPX2 was further validated in other datasets and found that it was more highly expressed in glioblastoma tumour tissue as compared to non-tumour brain tissue according to TCGA data (Figure 4F) and in BE-GICs from the HGCC cohort (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of the HGCC cohort shown in Figure 4G.

claim: High SRPX2 expression confers a worse prognosis.
source: Using survival data from the TCGA we also found that high SRPX2 expression confers a worse prognosis (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: A statistically significant lower number of nuclei per image field were found in both GIC19 and U3118 SRPX2 knockdown lines in invasion assays.
source: On average, a statistically significant lower number of nuclei per image field were found in both GIC19 and U3118 SRPX2 knockdown lines (Figure 4L) (p-value < 0.0001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from invasion assay experiments shown in Figure 4L.

claim: SRPX2 expression is predominantly in perivascular regions, including areas of microvascular proliferation and hyperplastic blood vessels, according to Ivy GAP data.
source: Interestingly, interrogation of the Ivy GAP (Puchalski et al., 2018) resource revealed SRPX2 expression predominantly in perivascular regions, including areas of microvascular proliferation and hyperplastic blood vessels, whilst it was down-regulated in the parenchymal leading edge and infiltrating tumour (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of Ivy GAP data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: SRPX2 was down-regulated in the parenchymal leading edge and infiltrating tumour according to Ivy GAP data.
source: Interestingly, interrogation of the Ivy GAP (Puchalski et al., 2018) resource revealed SRPX2 expression predominantly in perivascular regions, including areas of microvascular proliferation and hyperplastic blood vessels, whilst it was down-regulated in the parenchymal leading edge and infiltrating tumour (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of Ivy GAP data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: The scores for the peri/microvascular signature and the ACS were positively correlated in single tumour cells from scRNAseq data.
source: This showed that the scores for the peri/microvascular signature and the ACS were positively correlated (Figure 4N), whilst the former and the OPC signatures were not (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: The scores for the peri/microvascular signature and the OPC signatures were not correlated in single tumour cells from scRNAseq data.
source: This showed that the scores for the peri/microvascular signature and the ACS were positively correlated (Figure 4N), whilst the former and the OPC signatures were not (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: Proliferation was not affected by SRPX2 knockdown in GICs.
source: Proliferation was not affected by SRPX2 knockdown in GICs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from proliferation assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Less neurospheres formed in the U3118 shRNA SRPX2 knockdown line at lower cell counts.
source: Less neurospheres formed in the U3118 shRNA SRPX2 knockdown line at lower cell counts (6.25, 3.125, and 1.5625 cells per well) (Figure 4O, P), but this was not reproduced in the GIC19 shRNA SRPX2 knockdown lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from neurosphere assays shown in Figure 4O, P.

claim: The effect of SRPX2 knockdown on neurosphere formation was not reproduced in the GIC19 shRNA SRPX2 knockdown lines.
source: Less neurospheres formed in the U3118 shRNA SRPX2 knockdown line at lower cell counts (6.25, 3.125, and 1.5625 cells per well) (Figure 4O, P), but this was not reproduced in the GIC19 shRNA SRPX2 knockdown lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from neurosphere assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, J.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis performed on the lists of DEGs generated from the comparisons of BE-GICs versus nBE-GICs identified a deregulation of immune-related pathways – TGF-beta signalling and interferon-gamma signalling.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis performed on the lists of DEGs generated from the comparisons of BE-GICs versus nBE-GICs identified a deregulation of immune-related pathways – TGF-beta signalling and interferon-gamma signalling (Figure 3H), raising the possibility of differences in the tumour microenvironment of these glioblastomas.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from pathway analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: RARRES2 was significantly up-regulated in BE-GICs compared to nBE-GICs, in both the study's cohort and the HGCC cohort.
source: RARRES2 was found to be significantly up-regulated in BE-GICs compared to nBE-GICs, in both our cohort and the HGCC cohort, and in non-G-CIMP tumour tissue relative to non-tumour brain tissue (Figure 5A and B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: RARRES2 was significantly up-regulated in non-G-CIMP tumour tissue relative to non-tumour brain tissue.
source: RARRES2 was found to be significantly up-regulated in BE-GICs compared to nBE-GICs, in both our cohort and the HGCC cohort, and in non-G-CIMP tumour tissue relative to non-tumour brain tissue (Figure 5A and B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High expression of RARRES2 is correlated with a worse prognosis.
source: Moreover, high expression of RARRES2 is correlated with a worse prognosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from survival analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RARRES2 is well known to play a role in inflammation.
source: Significantly, RARRES2 is well known to play a role in inflammation (Mattern et al., 2014) and promoting the migration of plasmacytoid DC, macrophages, and NK-cells (Treeck et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: RARRES2 promotes the migration of plasmacytoid DC, macrophages, and NK-cells.
source: Significantly, RARRES2 is well known to play a role in inflammation (Mattern et al., 2014) and promoting the migration of plasmacytoid DC, macrophages, and NK-cells (Treeck et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The receptor CMKLR1 is expressed in tumour-associated macrophages from newly diagnosed GBMs in scRNAseq data.
source: In scRNAseq data from Pombo Antunes et al., 2021, and Neftel et al., 2019, the receptor CMKLR1 is expressed in tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) from newly diagnosed GBMs (Figure 5C, D), particularly in non-hypoxic TAMs (such as SEPP1-hi TAMs) as compared to hypoxic TAMs in recurrent glioblastomas (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: CMKLR1 is particularly expressed in non-hypoxic TAMs (such as SEPP1-hi TAMs) as compared to hypoxic TAMs in recurrent glioblastomas.
source: In scRNAseq data from Pombo Antunes et al., 2021, and Neftel et al., 2019, the receptor CMKLR1 is expressed in tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) from newly diagnosed GBMs (Figure 5C, D), particularly in non-hypoxic TAMs (such as SEPP1-hi TAMs) as compared to hypoxic TAMs in recurrent glioblastomas (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5E, F.

claim: The ACS/OPC pseudo-bulk score ratio had a significant positive correlation with the proportions of TAMs and of proliferating CD8 T cells.
source: The ACS/OPC pseudo-bulk score ratio had a significant positive correlation with the proportions of TAMs (in particular of SEPP1-hi moTAMs and cDC2) and of proliferating CD8 T cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5G, H.

claim: A significant negative correlation was found between the proportion of cancer cells and the ACS/OPC pseudo-bulk score ratio.
source: Conversely, a significant negative correlation was found between the proportion of cancer cells and the ACS/OPC pseudo-bulk score ratio (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Similar trends were observed when the proportion of TAMs, proliferating CD8 T cells, or cancer cells were correlated against the proportion of ACS-like tumour cells per patient.
source: Similar trends were observed when, utilising the single-cell resolution of the scRNAseq data, we correlated the proportion of TAMs, proliferating CD8 T cells, or cancer cells against the proportion of ACS-like tumour cells per patient (cells with higher ACS signature, compared to the two OPC signatures) (Figure 5J-L).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5J-L.

claim: The comparison of the proportion of ACS-like cancer cells against the fractions of monocytes and IFN-response CD8 T cells per patient yielded a significant positive correlation.
source: The comparison of the proportion of ACS-like cancer cells against the fractions of monocytes and IFN-response CD8 T cells per patient also yielded a significant positive correlation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: The results were reproduced when the signatures from Neftel et al., 2019, were used to determine the proportions of astrocyte-like cancer cells per patient and correlated to the proportions of immune and cancer cells in each tumour.
source: Furthermore, we show that these results were reproduced, when the signatures from Neftel et al., 2019, were used to determine the proportions of astrocyte-like cancer cells per patient and the latter were correlated to the proportions of immune and cancer cells in each tumour (Figure 5M-O).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from correlation analysis using Neftel et al. signatures shown in Figure 5M-O.

claim: Staining for CD68 in the FFPE tumour tissue from the study's cohort found a trend for an increased percentage of CD68+ cells in tumours of BE-GICs relative to nBE-GIC tumours.
source: Staining for CD68 in the FFPE tumour tissue from our cohort found a trend for an increased percentage of CD68+ cells in tumours of BE-GICs relative to nBE-GIC tumours (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A significant up-regulation of RARRES2 is identified in BE-GICs.
source: In conclusion, a significant up-regulation of RARRES2 is identified in BE-GICs, and an increased proportion of TAMs and CD8 proliferative T cells is found in tumours with a larger fraction of astrocyte-like tumour cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the differential expression analysis.

claim: An increased proportion of TAMs and CD8 proliferative T cells is found in tumours with a larger fraction of astrocyte-like tumour cells.
source: In conclusion, a significant up-regulation of RARRES2 is identified in BE-GICs, and an increased proportion of TAMs and CD8 proliferative T cells is found in tumours with a larger fraction of astrocyte-like tumour cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the scRNAseq correlation analysis.

claim: The composition of the TME may be different in tumours with an astrocytic signature enrichment.
source: This may indicate that the composition of the TME is different in tumours with an astrocytic signature enrichment.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the immune landscape findings.

claim: The G-CIMP hyper-methylator phenotype characterises IDH-mutant gliomas.
source: In particular, the G-CIMP hyper-methylator phenotype characterises IDH-mutant gliomas (Tahiliani et al., 2009), where mutated IDH gains the ability to convert α-KG to 2-HG, which functions as an oncometabolite whilst also being a competitive inhibitor of α-KG-dependent dioxygenases such as TET enzymes (Tahiliani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Mutated IDH gains the ability to convert α-KG to 2-HG, which functions as an oncometabolite whilst also being a competitive inhibitor of α-KG-dependent dioxygenases such as TET enzymes.
source: In particular, the G-CIMP hyper-methylator phenotype characterises IDH-mutant gliomas (Tahiliani et al., 2009), where mutated IDH gains the ability to convert α-KG to 2-HG, which functions as an oncometabolite whilst also being a competitive inhibitor of α-KG-dependent dioxygenases such as TET enzymes (Tahiliani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: IDH-mutant glioblastoma cells accumulate DNA methylation as TET enzymes are inhibited from removing methylation marks.
source: Consequently, IDH-mutant glioblastoma cells accumulate DNA methylation as TET enzymes are inhibited from removing methylation marks.
evidence: This is stated as an established mechanism with prior citation context.

claim: A hypo-methylation bias has been previously found in the paediatric H3 G34 mutant glioma subgroup.
source: A hypo-methylation bias has been previously found also in the paediatric H3 G34 mutant glioma subgroup (Sturm, 2012), where mutations in the histone H3 variant H3.3 (H3F3A) block SETD2 binding, leading to loss of H3K36 methylation, which in turn is linked to DNA methylation (Rose and Klose, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Mutations in the histone H3 variant H3.3 (H3F3A) block SETD2 binding, leading to loss of H3K36 methylation, which in turn is linked to DNA methylation.
source: A hypo-methylation bias has been previously found also in the paediatric H3 G34 mutant glioma subgroup (Sturm, 2012), where mutations in the histone H3 variant H3.3 (H3F3A) block SETD2 binding, leading to loss of H3K36 methylation, which in turn is linked to DNA methylation (Rose and Klose, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Mutation and loss of ATRX could contribute to hypo-methylation at highly repeated sequences such as rDNA.
source: Alternatively, mutation and loss of ATRX, which is consistently found in G34 mutant glioblastoma, could contribute to hypo-methylation at highly repeated sequences such as rDNA (Gibbons et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative mechanism with a supporting citation.

claim: A proportion of IDH-wildtype gliomas exhibited high percentages of hypo-methylated loci, which correlated with a stemness signature.
source: The pan-cancer analysis of DNA methylomes, published in 2018 (Saghafinia et al., 2018), reported that a proportion of IDH-wildtype gliomas exhibited high percentages of hypo-methylated loci, which correlated with a stemness signature (Malta et al., 2018), based on hypo-methylation of specific loci enriched for the SOX2-OCT4 binding motif.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The study did not find enrichment for the SOX2-OCT4 motif in the hypo-methylated DMRs from B-GICs.
source: We did not find enrichment for the SOX2-OCT4 motif in the hypo-methylated DMRs from B-GICs, but rather an enrichment for TF binding sites known to play a role in glial/astrocyte differentiation, which is consistent with the enrichment for an astrocytic signature.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Astrocyte differentiation requires Nfia-induced demethylation of key astrocyte lineage specifying genes.
source: Of particular interest was the finding of an enrichment for members of the NFI family in the hypo-methylated DMRs from B-GICs as previous studies have shown that astrocyte differentiation requires Nfia-induced demethylation of key astrocyte lineage specifying genes (Sanosaka et al., 2017; Namihira et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The methylome underpins the differentiation potential of NSCs rather than gene expression itself.
source: In fact, Sanosaka et al., 2017, showed that the methylome underpins the differentiation potential of NSCs rather than gene expression itself.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: E11.5 embryonic mouse NSCs were lineage-restricted and only giving rise to neurons.
source: They found that E11.5 embryonic mouse NSCs were lineage-restricted and only giving rise to neurons, whilst E18.5 NSCs had an increased proportion of hypo-methylated loci and were multipotent – being able to give rise to glial and neuronal lineages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: E18.5 NSCs had an increased proportion of hypo-methylated loci and were multipotent – being able to give rise to glial and neuronal lineages.
source: They found that E11.5 embryonic mouse NSCs were lineage-restricted and only giving rise to neurons, whilst E18.5 NSCs had an increased proportion of hypo-methylated loci and were multipotent – being able to give rise to glial and neuronal lineages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: DMRs with reduced methylation in E18.5 NSCs as compared to E11.5 NSCs are enriched for NFI binding sites.
source: Furthermore, this study also showed that DMRs with reduced methylation (hypo-methylated) in E18.5 NSCs as compared to E11.5 NSCs are enriched for NFI binding sites, and that this gene family was responsible for the loss of DNA methylation and gain of multipotency for the glial lineage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: The NFI gene family was responsible for the loss of DNA methylation and gain of multipotency for the glial lineage in E18.5 NSCs.
source: Furthermore, this study also showed that DMRs with reduced methylation (hypo-methylated) in E18.5 NSCs as compared to E11.5 NSCs are enriched for NFI binding sites, and that this gene family was responsible for the loss of DNA methylation and gain of multipotency for the glial lineage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: B-GICs may arise from a neural progenitor population that has undergone priming for glial differentiation, for example by the NFI TF family.
source: It is conceivable that B-GICs may arise from a neural progenitor population that has undergone priming for glial differentiation, for example by the NFI TF family.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Global methylation loss correlates with increased resistance to immunotherapy and immune evasion signatures.
source: A recent methylome analysis of various tumour types has found that global methylation loss correlates with increased resistance to immunotherapy and immune evasion signatures (Jung et al., 2019), hence the identification of GBMs with these features could have important implications in patient stratification for immunomodulatory treatments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.
